deep.reconstruction:
This page is the second page of Gauss's mathematical diary (Tagebuch, Cod. Ms. Gauss Math. 48). It holds the entries dated 26 May to 31 July 1796. These are short notes of results, not derivations. Below is the precise content of each entry, with my reconstruction of the implicit mathematics marked as such.

(a) 26 May. 'Scalam simplicem in seriebus varie recurrentibus esse functionem similem secundi ordinis scalarum componentium.' A 'scala' is de Moivre's 'scala relationis', i.e. the characteristic polynomial of a linear recurrent sequence. Take a series built from several recurrent series, e.g. termwise. Its simple scale is a symmetric ('similar') function of second order of the component scales. [Mine:] If u_k = sum A_i alpha_i^k and v_k = sum B_j beta_j^k, then w_k = u_k v_k satisfies the recurrence whose characteristic roots are the products alpha_i beta_j. Its coefficients are symmetric functions of the component coefficients.

(b) 31 May. 'Comparationes infinitorum in numeris primis et factoribus' (comparisons of infinities in primes and factors). This is asymptotic counting of primes and divisors; it foreshadows (f).

(c) 3 June. A scale for series whose terms are products, or indeed arbitrary functions, of the terms of any number of recurrent series. This generalises (a) to products and polynomial combinations of several linear recurrences.

(d) 5 June. Formula for the sum of the divisors of any composite number. The 'factor generalis' is (a^(n+1)-1)/(a-1). [Mine:] sigma(N) = prod over p^n || N of (p^(n+1)-1)/(p-1).

(e) 5 June. 'Periodorum summa omnibus infra modulum numeris pro elementis sumtis, fact. gen. ((n+1)a-n)a^(n-1).' [Mine:] Fix a modulus m and take each x in 1..m as 'element'. The multiples of x split Z/m into gcd(x,m) cosets ('periods'), each of length m/gcd(x,m). Summing the number of periods over all x gives P(m) = sum_{x=1}^m gcd(x,m). This is multiplicative, with P(p^n) = ((n+1)p - n) p^(n-1), exactly the stated factor. [Derivation, mine:] P(p^n) = sum_{k=0}^n p^k * phi(p^(n-k)) = p^n + n(p^n - p^(n-1)).

(f) 19 June. 'Leges distributionis' (laws of distribution). No content is given; probably about the distribution of primes or divisors.

(g) 20 June. 'Factorum summae in infinitum = pi^2/6 sum. Num.' [Mine:] sum_{k<=N} sigma(k) ~ (pi^2/6)(1+2+...+N) ~ pi^2 N^2/12. Sketch: sum_{k<=N} sigma(k) = sum_{d<=N} d*floor(N/d)... equivalently sum_{q<=N} sum_{d<=N/q} d ~ (N^2/2) sum 1/q^2 = (pi^2/6)(N^2/2).

(h) 22 June. He began to think about 'multipliers' connected with the forms of divisors of quadratic forms. These are the linear forms of prime divisors of x^2 - Dy^2, a precursor of character and genus theory.

(i) 27 June (starred). 'A new proof of the golden theorem (quadratic reciprocity) a priori, wholly different and quite elegant.' The diary gives no details.

(j) 3 July. 'Quaeque partitio numeri a in tria [squares] dat formam in bina [squares] separabilem.' [Mine:] A representation a = alpha^2+beta^2+gamma^2 yields a binary quadratic form of determinant -a. It is obtained from x^2+y^2+z^2 on the lattice orthogonal to (alpha,beta,gamma) (or its adjoint), and is decomposable as a sum of squares of linear forms. This is the correspondence later developed in Disquisitiones Arithmeticae (DA) arts. 278-292.

(k) Crossed out. 'Summa trium quadratorum continue proportionalium numquam primus esse potest...' [Mine:] Three squares in continued proportion are k^2a^4, k^2a^2b^2, k^2b^4. Their sum is k^2(a^4+a^2b^2+b^4) = k^2(a^2+ab+b^2)(a^2-ab+b^2). This is composite except when k=a=b=1, which gives the prime 3. That counterexample plausibly explains the deletion ('conspiciemus exemplum').

(l) 10 July (double star). 'EYPHKA num = Delta+Delta+Delta.' Every positive integer is a sum of three triangular numbers. Equivalently, 8n+3 is a sum of three odd squares; proved in DA art. 293 via the three-square theorem.

(m) Undated, between 10 and 16 July. Euler's determination of the forms in which composite numbers are contained more than once. These are Euler's numeri idonei (convenient numbers), treated in DA art. 303.

(n) 16 July. Principles for composing scales of variously recurrent series; a sequel to (a) and (c).

(o) 31 July. Euler's method for proving the relation between rectangles under the segments of intersecting chords of conic sections is applied to all curves. [Mine:] Through a point, draw secants in two fixed directions to an algebraic curve of degree n. The ratio of the products of the n segments on each secant depends only on the directions. This is Newton's theorem, generalising the intersecting-chords theorem for conics.
errors: In (e) the transcription '((n+1)a-na)a^{n-1}' must read ((n+1)a-n)a^{n-1}. Only this form is correct, as checked against sum gcd(x,p^n).
The crossed-out claim (k) is false for 1+1+1=3. Otherwise a^4+a^2b^2+b^4 always factors, so the deletion is consistent with spotting this single exception.
Entry (g) is an asymptotic statement written as an equality. 'Summae in infinitum' means the ratio tends to pi^2/6; it is correct in that sense.

results.what: Termwise products and combinations of linear recurrent sequences are again linear recurrent; their scale is a symmetric function of the component scales
results.modern_name: Closure of C-finite sequences under Hadamard product; Hadamard product of rational generating functions is rational
results.usually_credited_to: de Moivre/Euler/Lagrange for scales; formal closure theorems 19th-20th c. (Hadamard 1890s for products)

results.what: Sum over x mod m of the number of periods (gcd(x,m)) is multiplicative with factor ((n+1)p-n)p^(n-1)

results.modern_name: Average order of the divisor-sum function

results.what: Every integer is a sum of three triangular numbers
results.modern_name: Gauss's Eureka theorem (Fermat polygonal number theorem, case of triangular numbers)

results.what: New a priori proof of quadratic reciprocity
Representations as sums of three squares correspond to binary forms of determinant -a
Forms in which composites are represented more than once
Intersecting-chords relation extended from conics to all algebraic curves
results.modern_name: Newton's theorem on products of secant segments (later generalised by Carnot)

deep.surprise_reason: This page is Gauss's well-known, published diary (Klein 1903; Werke X.1; Gray 1984), so all entries are known as his. The only mildly notable point is that entry (e) can be read precisely as Pillai's gcd-sum function with its exact multiplicative formula, about 140 years before Pillai. Whether commentators state this explicitly is unsure.

checkable.sympy: all(sum(gcd(x,p**n) for x in range(1,p**n+1)) == ((n+1)*p-n)*p**(n-1) for p in [2,3,5,7] for n in range(1,5))
checkable.asserts: Entry 5 Jun: the gcd-sum function equals ((n+1)p-n)p^(n-1) at prime powers

checkable.sympy: all(divisor_sigma(p**n) == (p**(n+1)-1)/(p-1) for p in [2,3,5] for n in range(1,6))
N=20000; abs(sum(divisor_sigma(k) for k in range(1,N+1))/(N*(N+1)/2) - pi**2/6).evalf() < 0.01
checkable.asserts: Sum of sigma(k) up to N over the sum of the numbers 1..N tends to pi^2/6

checkable.asserts: EUREKA: every n is a sum of three triangular numbers
Sum of three squares in continued proportion factors, hence is prime only for 1+1+1=3 (crossed-out entry)

checkable.asserts: Termwise product (square) of a recurrent series is recurrent with scale of product roots: F_k^2 satisfies x^3-2x^2-2x+1

transcription_corrections: Entry 3 Jul: the image appears to read 'in tria □' (three squares) for the partition of a, not 'in bina □'. The resulting form is then 'in bina □ separabilem'.
'Coefficientes ... per radicum potestatis additas' on the previous page should be 'potestatum summas'; 'separabilitem' should be 'separabilem'.
